speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before the house adjourned at six o'clock I listened with interest to the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) who went through his normal ranting and raving as he usually does-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Is the minister intending to raise a point of order with respect to the amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak on the amendment.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Then I will place the amendment before the house. Mr. Martin (Essex East) seconded by Mr. Mcllraith moved:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"Bill No. C-52 be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of amending clause 10 to include the promotion of employment as one of the specific objects of the council."

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
As I began to say, before the house rose at six o'clock I listened with a great deal of interest to what is becoming known as the usual ranting and raving of the hon. member for Essex East on his favourite subject, using the same speech as he so often uses, with its tossed salad type of verbiage. The hon. member said that this government took three years before it brought about any conference on unemployment in this country. His memory is short. If he thinks

Productivity Council
back to July, 1958 he will recall that I called a conference here in Ottawa. Representatives of labour, agriculture, industry and other important segments of our economy gathered here to discuss the problem of unemployment at that time. As a result of that conference the municipal winter works program was inaugurated that fall, and the success of that program has continued ever since that time.
The hon. member talked about the unemployment situation in Canada and said it is not right to compare it with the situation in any other country on the North American continent. Let me inform him that in the United States at this moment there is something like 6.4 per cent of the labour force unemployed-well over four million people-[DOT] and most certainly we have a relationship with that country across the border, and whatever happens in the United States is bound to affect our economy.
1 would point out also that there are always two sides to the picture and we must not forget this positive aspect of our economy, namely that there are more people employed now than ever before in the history of this country on a month to month basis. As to a comparison between November of 1960 and November of 1959, I may say there are some 99,000 more people employed in this country this year than there were last year.
It depends on the viewpoint one takes. There is always a positive and a negative side to a question. We have not said we do not recognize the serious situation presented by unemployment, and this is borne out by the measures which this government has taken since we came to office in 1957 and 1958. This session certainly shows that this government is well aware of the current situation, because each and every measure which has been brought before the house has been designed for the sole purpose of providing employment and bolstering the economy of this country.
The hon. member for Essex East in presenting his amendment finds himself in his usual position of watching the parade go by and then having to run to catch up with it. I remember reading a report of a debate in the thirties when the hon. member was on the government side of the house. It was a debate on unemployment in this chamber and when one of the members from Toronto, Mr. Massey, was speaking, the hon. member for Essex East said: Let us get this over; I have a train to catch. The hon. member has been catching trains ever since; he has been in a hurry ever since.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: I always got there.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
You left the unemployment debate to catch that train, too.
The hon. gentleman talks about unemployment in Windsor. Let me say that the figures show that ever since he was elected to be a member of parliament for Windsor, that is when unemployment started in that city. What did the hon. gentleman say in 1954 when Ford was moving to Oakville? Did he raise his voice and say they should not undermine the industrial position of that city?

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: The minister has asked me a question. He asked me what I did.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I can answer the question because I know the facts. Anyway the hon. member for Essex East is not happy about the present bill. He is not happy about the other bills that have been brought before the house, either. He is not happy with any of the measures which the government has evolved in order to maintain a stable economy and provide employment. Let me say this: I have a strong suspicion that there will be no satisfying the hon. member for Essex East, no matter what this government does. I think he is resolved at all costs to maintain his position of not being satisfied with anything. I think the hon. member has in his make-up a sort of gloating, gleeful personality which seems to gloat at any undermining of our economy because, as has been said by one of the hon. member's friends who is preparing to be a candidate for the Liberal party, the only way the Liberal party can assume power again is through a depression in this country.
In any event, the attitude of the hon. member for Essex East is completely negative, destructive and obstructionist. Let me advise him that he would go a lot further in carrying out the role of a reasonable and constructive member of the opposition if, from time to time at least, he could bring himself to admit that some of the things the government is doing have some prospect of being useful and successful. I honestly believe that in his heart the hon. member realizes that this government has been endeavouring to do everything in its power to help the economic situation. If not, why does the hon. member vote for these measures? Why does he place on them his stamp of approval by voting for them after spending so much time rehashing the same old speech he gives in this house from time to time?

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: It is puny, but one more step; and late, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
One of the measures recently approved by this house was the housing measure. The hon. member for Essex East

said it was a good measure but that he had some grave doubts about its effectiveness. Let me assure the hon. gentleman that he should' not have had any doubts about it because action in this field is already taking place. Let me refer to the following article in this evening's issue of the Ottawa Citizen:
Ottawa Seeks Sewage Loan-$10 Million.
Ottawa will seek a loan of $10 million from the federal government to expedite completion of a $20 million sewage disposal project.
Mayor Nelms said the move is to take advantage of new federal legislation under which loans amounting to two-thirds of the total cost for sewage disposal projects can be secured, and under which 25 per cent of the total cost of works finished by March, 1963, will be rebated.
"This will save Ottawa approximately $2,500,000," the mayor emphasized.
Here is an example of direct action that has been taken as a result of the direct and immediate action taken by this government. A recent issue of the Ottawa Citizen carried an article under the headline "Plan 350 Homes for Low Incomes" which reads in part as follows:
A plan to provide low cost housing for people in the low income brackets was submitted to board of control by Robert Campeau, president of Campeau Construction Company Limited.
Mr. Campeau told the board he planned the construction of 350 housing units on the old Arkell farm lying between Pinecrest and the Walkley roads south of the Queensway.
Mr. Campeau is reported as having said:
"It has been said private enterprises would not provide low cost housing for people in the low income brackets," Mr. Campeau said. "Now because of the favourable financing provided by the federal government, through C.M.H.C., we are able to do, on terms comparable with city schemes for low rental, full recovery projects."
He said he already had 200 applications for the low cost housing. The salary range for people applying is from $3,800 to $4,500, he advised the board.
He added that the provision of services would be carried by the subdivider in relation to all facilities save a trunk sewer.
There is another indication of what is happening as a result of the legislation this government introduced.
Let us take a look at what is being done in the field of vocational and technical schools. As soon as third reading was given to the bill in this house the government of Ontario announced a $8 million program to be started immediately under this plan.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: They had that in mind before, and the minister knows it. It was in the speech from the throne.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
That, Mr. Speaker, is an answer to the hon. member for Essex East who said that the legislation concerning vocational training and technical schools would not bring immediate results in the form of jobs.
Productivity Council

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: May I direct a question to the minister? Is it not a fact that the $8 million referred to is half the quota until March 31, 1967 according to the minister's own words the other day?

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman looking for another headline?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
It amounts to a great deal more than $8 million. It is going to be a very large program undertaken by all the provinces across this country amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars as a result of this legislation. That is only a start. I say that all the measures we have been bringing forward are already having their effects. The hon. member for Essex East has singled out only four measures. He did not even have the patience to wait to see the whole program before condemning it. As a matter of fact he is condemning the program in advance.
In his attitude the hon. member for Essex East reminds me somewhat of a small boy at Christmas time who rushes in, tears all the wrapping off the presents and then sets up a howl that what was in the boxes was not what he wanted. I submit the simple truth is that the hon. member did not get his little red wagon, Mr. Speaker. In the case of the hon. gentleman he cannot even wait until Christmas but has to start howling even before the packages are unwrapped. I say that is not a responsible attitude.
Let us now look at the hon. member's amendment. I submit this is not a serious amendment. In the first place the inclusion of the phrase which the hon. member so strenuously urges is unnecessary as I pointed out at the committee stage. I attempted to make it clear that the purpose of this bill is set out in the preamble. When you have a whole series of bills one of whose main objects is the promotion of employment you surely do not have to spell out that phrase in every bill. That is what the measures are all about. They are designed to bolster our economy. That is what they are intended to do. They are intended to promote employment, all of them. To stick that phrase into every bill like a raisin in a fruit cake will not in any way alter or improve the effectiveness of these measures.
We submit that these measures will be effective and that in the main they will have an immediate effect. Certainly they will have a continuity of effectiveness in the years to come. These are co-ordinating measures. They are partnership measures with the provinces, the municipalities and other interested bodies in this country.
All of these measures are a part of the program and each one, I submit, is designed to deal with a specific problem in our

Productivity Council
economy. Unemployment is an economic problem, there is no question about it. It must be cured by economic measures. That is the only way it will be cured. I submit it is not a problem which can be cured by the insertion of pious phrases in our bills. We have tried to avoid pious phrases.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: This whole bill has no content at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
We have brought forward
measures which will put into action the immense economic forces in this country.
In answer to what has been said now, I say there is nothing easier than being destructive. It is easy to get up and say in tones of righteous wrath that this is no good and that is no good. We saw an exhibition of that this afternoon. I think all hon. members recognized the righteous wrath that is usually displayed by the hon. member for Essex East. The hon. member denounced this as no good and that as no good but there was not an indication from him as to what is good. The only suggestion we ever get concerns the setting up of 20 or 22 various committees across the country.
I believe it requires a degree of constructive responsibility to analyse and appraise these measures on their merits and to judge them by their results. As I pointed out earlier, results are already quite evident. I submit there is a favourable response across Canada to all these measures and immediate action is being brought about. I invite hon. members to consider that public confidence is being maintained despite all the words, actions and hopes of hon. members opposite to the contrary.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: The minister is certainly wearing rose-coloured glasses.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. member suggests that I am wearing rose-coloured glasses but at least we on this side of the house can see through them and we are taking measures to rectify whatever we see that is wrong.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: How can a blind man see?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I submit that the productivity council will be useful. I have every faith that it will be a useful council and I have no doubt of the usefulness of such a body in our economy. Certainly, by itself-and I have pointed this out-it will not solve the problem, but we have a number of these measures and when they are put together we have every hope that they will have the desired effect upon our economy. I am sure that they will be beneficial and useful to the people of this country.

Let us examine the position of the hon. member for Essex East. He says the bill is no good; it will have no effect, but he will vote for it.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: For the reasons given.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
He says there are all kinds of things wrong with this bill, but all of the weaknesses will vanish automatically when we put into the bill the phrase that he suggests, "promotion of employment". If we only include those words, all the weaknesses will vanish. All we have to do is to put in these three words and the bill will be perfect because he has submitted the amendment. In other words, what I think the hon. member for Essex East is trying to do is to climb aboard, and he is using this method to do it.
What will this bill do, Mr. Speaker? It will set up a council; that is, a body on which will be represented some of the leading people in our country. It will have on it representatives of all segments of our economic activity. I wish to say that the effort and the aim of this government is to mobilize the economy against insecurity. We are mobilizing the economy on all levels, federal, provincial, municipal, business, industry, agriculture, labour; nobody is left out and nothing is being left out. To do this, in order to bring about this mobilization, we are bringing in measures in the field of housing, construction, municipal aid, the economy, small business, exports, the training of workers, and so on.
I think the hon. member for Essex East will agree that in the main they are all good things. He has some doubts, and possibly hopes that they will not be as effective as we think they will be, and as we hope they will be. Of course, that is something that he has to decide in his own conscience.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: On a point of order, I do not mind what the hon. gentleman says about my arguments but under our rules he has no right to suggest that I have acted in anything but good faith and in accordance with my conscience.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: That is the trouble.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: It is a well established principle of debate that hon. members must assume that their fellow members, like themselves, are acting in good faith and from proper motives.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
That is right; I left it up to the hon. member to decide according to his own conscience. I did not accuse him, or say anything different.

These programs that we have brought forward, calling for the construction of new homes with low down payments, have never been experienced before in this country; programs call for the construction of new training schools; the clearing away of slum areas in our great cities, improvement in the standard of residences and home improvements for our Canadian people; for aid to universities and municipalities and aid to young people, aid for students who wish to advance themselves in the industrial life; the construction of sewage disposal plants across Canada for the preservation of our water resources.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Is this something that the minister is reading from a prepared text?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: The programs call for an opportunity for Canadian businessmen to expand; they call for an opportunity for Canadian businessmen to go into the export markets around the world and to compete there on equal terms through the provision of adequate credit. I submit, Mr. Speaker, this is no "pie in the sky" approach; this is a straightforward, down to earth approach to deal with the problem.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Pious talk.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: It is also a common-sense approach which will bolster up our economy where it is lagging. It will give opportunity to our young people who have not had a chance to acquire a formal education, and it will help business, labour and industry.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the peroration of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) sounded very much like a second edition of the vision and suggests to me once again that instead of having a program of substance the government has given the greatest amount of attention to window dressing and to the package in which its program is being wrapped.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: You should know all about window dressing.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I think the amendment before the house is a straightforward one; it merely calls on the house to express the opinion that in the legislation to set up the productivity council the objective of the work of the productivity council should be the promotion of employment. If we take that as an objective, together with the suggestion that we in this party have made that the productivity council should have the right to make recommendations to the government, we might then be on the way to establishing a body that could take a very active part in assuring full employment and full production.
Productivity Council
I think the Minister of Labour would be much more helpful to the government if he spent less time in demolishing the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and more time in presenting to the house and the country the facts with regard to the government's own program. I suggest the time has come when the Minister of Labour should tell parliament and the country exactly what the government expects will be the result by way of additional employment that flows from all of the projects and all of the legislation that have been presented to parliament at the present time.
We are in a very serious situation in Canada. The government can talk in glib and glowing terms of its action; the fact remains that each passing day that this government has occupied the treasury benches, now for a period of three years, the unemployment situation has become worse. The situation now, according to the latest information, is so bad that we have a higher rate of unemployment than we had in any time during the last 15 years.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: I wonder whether the hon. member would permit a question. I think he is under a misapprehension when he says the last 15 years because surely he is not suggesting it was worse in 1944. It is just for 15 years that we have had these figures.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate will know that at that time demobilization was taking place and there were other reasons why people were looking for work.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: The other reason was the Liberal party.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
We do not want to go too far
back for the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate because his party occupied the treasury benches during a very difficult period of time when they were just as unsuccessful in meeting employment requirements as the present government has been in recent years.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Wait till Tommy Douglas gets in ahead of you.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: The unemployment figure demonstrates not only the number of people who are unemployed in Canada but is an indication of the tremendous loss in production that has taken place as the result of the widespread unemployment. The fact of the matter is that in the last year we have lost by way of production between $1.5 billion and $2 billion of wealth, and so there is a great challenge to the government-

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Can you prove that?

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
-to produce a program that will, in the words of the Minister of Labour,

Productivity Council mobilize the economy against insecurity. The Minister of Labour will not justify his program or his lack of a program by talking about the large numbers of persons now employed. It is not much comfort to the hundreds of thousands who are unemployed to know that there are more employed persons now than there have been in the past. The government's program will be justified when the unemployed have an opportunity to work.
The minister and the government have talked about an over-all program. I want to say that we have been pleased to support this bits and pieces program, this inadequate program, this beginning of a program to meet the present difficulty. There are many other things that I suggest should be done. I think the government should now accept a principle that was enunciated during the war and was accepted by the nation as a whole, namely that anything physically possible would be made financially possible. I think it is physically possible to put Canadians to work and the government should be undertaking those steps that would make this financially possible.
I suggest that there should be established in our country at this time a great capital development fund in the hands of and controlled and operated by the federal government to be used for investment in Canadian industry, to be used for investment in depressed areas and to be used to stimulate our economy, to prime the pump with the objective of bringing about full employment. I suggest also that the government, in co-operation with the provinces, should be prepared at this time to assist in a massive public works program. The federal government has taken certain action in this session to stimulate public works. The fact is that many provincial governments are faced with such budgetary difficulties that they may be compelled to cut back provincial expenditures and thus the provincial governments through no fault of their own will undo much of the valuable work that is being done by the federal government.
The minister talked about the over-all program that the government had presented. He went over the various things that had been done. I suggest that in addition to this program the government should bring into operation once again the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act which was placed on the statute books in 1938 and under which at that time federal money for public works was provided to municipalities at a rate of 2 per cent. This is the kind of far-reaching program for the development of municipal projects that should be brought about at this time, and it should be the purpose and the duty of the productivity council to inquire


into the situation and to make recommendations resulting in the promotion of employment as set forth in the legislation before the house.
The minister talks about his program. I am now trying to suggest to him things that should be added to his program. I suggest that now is the time for the federal government to co-operate with the provinces in a national highway program. Now is the time for the government to cease being content with a contribution to a very limited trans-Canada highway program. The minister has asked for suggestions. He has asked for comments. I suggest that now is the time for the government to undertake measures to bolster farm income which would result in a greater demand for the products of our factories. Now is the time for the government to proceed with its well known commitment to provide for Canada an old age security system which would allow persons to retire on an adequate income.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Order. The hon. member is following in a debate which has been fairly wide but surely there are some limits to what may be discussed on an amendment which only seeks to refer the bill back to the committee to add a clause to section 10 to include in the council's powers the promotion of employment. While I have not objected to the hon. member speaking about employment and unemployment, when he gets into farm income, the trans-Canada highway and other matters it seems to me that a line has to be drawn.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would suggest with great deference that the house listened to the Minister of Labour outline the government's broad program without any objection. He talked about such things as the government measure to provide loans for small business. He talked about the housing program, which is not contained in this legislation. He talked about other measures that the government has brought forward and he challenged the opposition to put forward suggestions. I suggest with great deference that if it is in order for the Minister of Labour to go far beyond the scope of the bill and far beyond the scope of the amendment then, no objection having been raised, the same kind of latitude should be extended to other members in replying to his statement, particularly in view of the fact that he issued a challenge to opposition members to put forward alternative suggestions.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not think I could accept what the hon. member says in total. I have no objection to the hon. member dealing with the matters raised by the hon. member for Essex East and the Minister of Labour

in this debate, that is, the program that the government has brought before the house. Even though that is out of order in this debate it has been discussed, but I do think that a line should be drawn short of the fields to which the hon. member referred.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: I wonder whether I could speak to the point of order and try to assist my hon. friend who is in obvious difficulty. On the government's own figures there has been a considerable drop in agricultural employment over a period amounting to some 300,000. Over the last decade the figure is some 25 per cent less in spite of an increase in production. It would seem to me that because of that circumstance it is not proper for us under our procedures to differentiate between employment in one sector of the Canadian economy as opposed to another. While the hon. gentleman who is speaking is not always in order, I think this is one of the rare occasions when he is.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend from Essex East for his very great assistance. While it was said I am rarely in order I think my batting average is better than that of the hon. member for Essex East. None the less I accept his offer of assistance in the spirit in which it has been given, particularly in view of the fact we must acknowledge his authority in the field of agriculture, soybeans and other related matters.
Now, Mr. Speaker, your ruling was a very interesting one, namely that it is all right to be out of order in fields governed by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) but one must not get out of order in fields outside of those which are of concern to the Minister of Labour.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman accept a question at this point?

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Fine.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like the hon.
gentleman-I should like the hon. member for Essex East to pay particular attention -to answer this question. What would the hon. member, who I understand expects some day to head the new party, assess as the federal responsibility for today's unemployment?

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: I think it has been accepted by every political party, and politically by the party to which the hon. member belongs, that it is not only the duty of the federal government but it is the obligation of that government to bring about a full employment economy, just as the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has said in the past.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
No, no.
Productivity Council

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: He said, if I am elected prime minister no one will suffer from unemployment. Since he has been elected there has been more suffering from unemployment than at any other time.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to bring forward some further suggestions that I hope the government will consider as measures which would assist in bringing about a full employment economy. The Minister of Labour referred to the government's housing program, and took great credit for the results he said would flow from that program. I would suggest that the government's housing program has been inadequate and that in the areas of low rental housing, in the provision of housing for senior citizens, it has been very inadequate indeed.
The measure before us would ask the council to inquire inito the development of improved production and distribution methods. We endeavoured, when the house was in committee of the whole, to introduce an amendment which would have widened the scope of the bill and provided for an inquiry into methods to increase markets. I think that is something that this council should consider also. It is not just a question of increasing productivity to bring about full employment, it is a question of developing the markets that are necessary for the products of our industry.
If I may say so at this time, I want to express support for those steps that have been taken by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees).

I was saying I support the measures that have been taken by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the calling of the trade commissioners together to assist in the development of markets for Canadian products. While I expect to have more to say on this particular point at a later time, I feel that the development of markets is essential and that the provision of 20,000 baby chicks for Cuba, reference to which I have seen, is not that kind of expansion of our export trade to Cuba that would require any criticism or opposition from the Liberal party.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that in any inquiry into improved production and distribution methods this council will be forced to look

Productivity Council
at the costs taring our industry today. I think there is nothing that is causing more difficulty, causing higher production costs for the basic industries of our nation at this time than the high interest policy that is being followed by the government. The high interest rates that are prevalent in our country today are making it difficult for our industries to reach their maximum efficiency. The high interest rate coupled with the premium on the Canadian dollar is causing monetary and exchange difficulties that create a great burden for Canadian industry. This is the kind of overhaul of Canadian monetary policy that will be necessary if industries in our country are to reach their most efficient productivity.
What the government has done, Mr. Speaker, has been, useful. What the government has done is no substitute for implementing its promises to the Canadian people to provide job opportunities for all of those who are unemployed.

I cannot imagine any colder comfort than the speeches-if they get around to reading them -of the hon. member for Essex East and the hon. member for Assiniboia. There was an attempt at a last minute amendment which was immediately discarded by its own sponsor who said that notwithstanding the fact that the bill is not a good bill, it was a good bill. The theory implicit in this argument put up by the hon. lady and by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is that an increase in productivity at this time will reduce employment. The hon. lady nods her head in agreement, and I am glad that I did her no disservice. But, surely, the result of improving our productivity is to put ourselves in a position where the product of Canadian industry is saleable in world markets, and thereby to increase employment. How else is it to be done? You must improve productivity first of all.
What has the government said? It has said: we shall bring together broadly representative members of industry and commerce, organized labour, agriculture and members of the general public to give the body a leavening of broad interest. We want to bring about a condition in which productivity is improved in order to add to employment in Canada. In this respect it is in line with other measures which have been brought before us during the present session. Consider the National Housing Act. The hon. member for Assiniboia says it is not sufficient. That act has provided a great deal of employment in Canada through a mixture of public and private action by a government which is not fearful of entering into new fields, but will not go down the path of socialist embrace in which all freedom is destroyed.
I see the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) nod his head. I had some things to say about his philosophy during the last session. He nods his head. I was not at Calgary last week, so I do not know where he stood last week, but, surely, we have seen some amazing gyrations in which the far left is suddenly trying to embrace private enterprise. A few moments ago, the minister gave us a list of those measures. He told us that those four measures would increase employment in Canada, and thus decrease the number of the jobless. I must say that it is most confusing to listen to the speeches of hon. members on the government benches. Mr. Speaker, it is high time that the government take action, not by merely introducing legislation which will serve as a basis for the settlement of the economic problem, but rather by taking the necessary steps to settle that problem once and for all.
We convened last fall to enact a program which according to the Prime Minister himself, has been ready since September 21. Well, let him submit it to this parliament right now. The minister, a moment ago, referred to the housing legislation. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that we have been taunted from the very moment this bill was placed before the house, whether on second reading, or in committee, in other words constantly. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) and other ministers, and even certain hon. members have said to us: "And you will support the bill".
Well, my reply is quite simple. Mr. Speaker, I was elected to the legislature in 1934, in the darkest days of the depression, when the Conservative government was in power in Ottawa, from 1930 to 1935. I have seen what unemployment means. I perfectly remember the time when people, in groups of 25 to 50, would gather on my verandah in the morning waiting to ask their member for help to buy food, or to be given blankets for their children. I distinctly remember those days and I also know that no Canadian would

want to go through them again. However, I fear that unless the government reaches an early decision on means of correcting the present situation, we will soon be faced with a situation similar to the thirties.
Some will ask why we will support the bill if we think it does not include the provisions needed to settle the problem. To those people I say this: when a jobless man has nothing to eat and is offered hardtack instead of bread, he will take the hardtack. If he is offered treacle instead of maple syrup, he will [DOT]accept the treacle.
Mr. Speaker, let it be understood that if we support these measures, it is because we want to help the government find an answer to the problem. We want to let the government lay the foundation of its program, because that is what the government calls it, a foundation. However, we want more action.
The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Morris) has referred to the Gordon report. He managed to find bombastic statements to fill in an empty speech.

Now, Mr. Speaker, it may be trite to say that I am rather unhappy with this bill. I

must go further and say that the situation has not improved as the debate on the bill has progressed. We have seen complete contradictions by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees), the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) even contradicted himself. We have seen vigorous resistance by the government to every attempt to improve this bill. In fact I might say that if the government of the day would attack the problems of the day with the same vigour with which they resist any improvements in their legislation, then we might not be faced with the problems we have today.
We have been told that if we fail to find anything in the bill all we have to do is look in the preamble and we will find it there. As we know, the preamble to any bill is a sort of catchall. In fact, it reminds me very much of some words written by Mr. Wilson MacDonald, when he made reference to the speaker at a service club meeting and went on in these words:
And if the interest seemed to lag He praised the clergy and the flag,
He lauded surgeons and their knives,
He blessed all mothers and all wives.
His talk was like a soothing drug That made men want to kiss and hug;
Or give one hundred thousand bucks To under-privileged woodchucks,
Who got this way, now here's the rub, Because the motto of this club Was ever this-the thought quite missed 'em- That no one must destroy the System.
We have also seen introduced in this bill a brand new principle about which I am certainly not very happy. Under quite close interrogation the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) finally admitted that it is a brand new principle and that it was the first time it had ever been tried in this country. I refer to the system of double taxation on the general taxpayers. That is certainly a novel system of taxation and I do not think it is a good one.
As has been mentioned by innumerable members on the government side, there are in this bill some good measures-I will make that admission-and over a long period of time some good may come out of this bill that is before us today. However, we cannot escape the facts. One of the facts that we cannot get around is that in the United States and Canada at the present time we have the highest productivity of any place in the world; but at the same time that we have the highest productivity we are the only two countries in the western world with an unemployment problem. The reason that we have this problem in these two countries of highest productivity is that we have not given any consideration to the problems that arise through having the highest productivity.

The export powers under the existing act may be summarized under four headings. Those four headings are:
(a)	To establish a list of countries, exports to which shall be subject to licence.
(b)	To control exports of arms, munitions, war materials or supplies.
(c)	To control exports of commodities where this is necessary to ensure adequate supply and distribution within Canada, and
(d)	To control exports where this is necessary to implement intergovernmental arrangements or commitments.
In 1958 it was found necessary to revise the export control list and I made an announcement in the house on August 16, at that time tabling the revised list which subsequently was printed in the Canada Gazette on August 27. When I made my statement in the house I pointed out that we were revising our export control list in conformity with the agreed new strategic list. On that occasion, as reported at page 3649 of Hansard, I said:

I went on to list a number that had been dropped from the former export control list. I then went on to say:
The export control list, moreover, serves an important function in indicating those items which are regarded as strategic, and an endeavour has been made to set forth the list in such form that traders may use it for this purpose.

Mr. Speaker, a similar question was in the mind of the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Stinson) who directed notice to me in this regard.
I think I should mention in general the situation in the Congo. Recent reports of developments there are most disturbing. During the past few days the security council has been discussing the Congo situation as a matter of urgency. A deadlock has now developed in the security council, and the general assembly will be required to resume its consideration of the matter.
I think I could say nothing further than this. As Mr. Hammarskjold said in July, the United Nations through its operations and its action in the Congo has been given its greatest opportunity in history. I hope there will not be carried into effect the threatened withdrawals of national representatives in the United Nations forces. To do so can lead only to more chaotic conditions in that country.
As to any consideration being given on the part of Canada to increasing its forces, I may say that such consideration has not been given. Canada has been generous in the contributions it has made to the United Nations and to the United Nations forces. At

the present time I can only say that no consideration is being given to any additional forces to meet a situation created by the anticipated withdrawal of certain national troops.

On September 26 I brought before the United Nations assembly the question of the creation of an experts' bank. The Canadian delegation has brought this matter before the assembly in two resolutions. The first, which Canada took the initiative in presenting, places the existing United Nations arrangements for providing operational and executive experts to underdeveloped countries on a permanent basis. This received the support of the assembly. The second, dealing with arrangements to facilitate the prompt supply of technical assistance personnel to underdeveloped countries, was adopted unanimously. It recommends that governments consider the desirability and feasibility, within their own constitutional and administrative structures, of establishing and maintaining reserves of qualified personnel available for assignment by the United Nations to advisory or operational technical assistance posts.
This experts' bank, if mobilized, if accepted not only in principle but translated into reality, would provide in the days ahead for the instant mobilization of technical assistance.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, December 14, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-52, to establish a national productivity council-Mr. Hees-Mr. Flynn in the chair.
On clause 10-Objects and powers.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Order. When the committee rose last night we were considering
Productivity Council
clause 10, and more especially the amendment by the hon. member for Timmins, which I need not read again.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make one or two observations about the hon. member's amendment, along the lines that were made just before the committee rose yesterday by the hon. member for Laurier, who at that time read the words of the Prime Minister, which I am sure I do not need to repeat now, that the government would welcome any suggestions for the improvement of this bill.
It is surely evident that if this productivity council is to have any real impact upon the Canadian economy, it must have the power to make recommendations to industry, to labour, and above all, in the broader field, to make recommendations to the government. It seems to me that since there has been a good deal of confusion between statements by the different ministers, by the sponsor of the bill, the godfather of the bill and the stepfather of the bill, who seem to be unable to agree about the purposes and objectives of the bill, it seems to me that at least this one point might be clarified, and clarified completely.
If I seem to exaggerate; if anyone thinks I am exaggerating when I say there are differences in view as to the very basic purpose of this council, I would draw hon. members' attention to the original statement at the resolution stage by the sponsor of the bill, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who, under the doctrine of collective responsibility, presumably was speaking for the whole government then as no doubt he was on another occasion when he described certain people in this country as wonderful people. On this occasion when he was speaking about this bill the Minister of Trade and Commerce said, as recorded on page 566 of Hansard for December 6:
The national council should act as a policy making body . ..
Then the Prime Minister, speaking on second reading on behalf of the absent Minister of Trade and Commerce and, I might add, speaking instead of the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce, had this to say, as found on page 750 of Hansard for December 13:
I know we shall welcome any ideas or suggestions that may lead to any improvement in the bill, providing those suggestions are not of such a nature as would, in effect, constitute the council as a policy making body...
Whom do you believe, the Prime Minister who says that this council must not be constituted as a policy making body or the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who in first putting forward that it was expedient

Productivity Council
to introduce a bill for this purpose said that this national council should act as a policy making body? Which of these gentlemen is speaking the real mind of the government, or has the government any mind in this matter at all?
It seems to me this is a question that should be resolved on this clause which deals with the purposes of the council. Whether or not the council is a policy making body, it is obviously there to do something; and how it can do anything that will be effective unless its power to make recommendations is clear, explicit and unqualified is very hard to see. For that reason I am happy to support the amendment of the hon. member for Timmins.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, now that the minister has had a chance to think about this matter overnight, would he indicate to us whether he is prepared to accept the amendment? It might save any further remarks on my part.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: I gave the reasons why the government cannot accept the amendment, and I have had no reason to change that attitude overnight.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in order to explain the problem raised by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate may I say that I have had occasion to read Hansard and to study the remarks of the minister, and I note something in his remarks that may explain the strange phenomenon that confronts us at the present time. If hon. members will look at page 807 of Hansard for December 14 they will find that the minister stated, near the bottom of the page:
... this and other measures that will be brought down are part and parcel of a program to take care of the federal share of responsibility in this field and which will create an atmosphere that will give employment to these people.
This is the first time I have ever heard of employment being provided by an atmosphere. I therefore looked at the dictionary definition of the word, because I thought possibly there was a definition with which I was not familiar. Among the various definitions of "atmosphere" I find that one is "air" and another has reference to the normal pressure of the air at sea level being about 15 pounds per square inch.
In view of the completely opposite views of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Prime Minister, as outlined by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, maybe there is a little too much air involved in the bill and there should be a little more substance. Again, if we refer to the remarks of the Minister of Labour as found on page 802

of Hansard, we find that he had this to say with regard to the amendment now before us:
There is no provision in the bill which says the council cannot make recommendations to the government. Consequently it is my opinion that if, in the belief of this council, the over-all effect of its work could be improved with more beneficial results for all Canadians as a result of some action of the federal government, this council would be free to make such recommendations and suggestions, and these would be welcomed and given consideration.
In my view this is a very strange procedure. Are we to assume that just because there is nothing in the bill preventing the council from doing any particular thing, the council is free to do that thing? This is certainly a new procedure in the setting up of councils of this kind. I suggest it is much more appropriate that provision should be made for the council to make recommendations, because from past experience I would say that unless this power is given to them the hands of the members of the council will be tied, for all practical purposes, from the point of view of any recommendations they might make on the basis of the vast amount of knowledge that will be available to them. I would ask the minister to reconsider the matter to see if he cannot agree that this amendment would definitely be an improvement to the bill.
Amendment (Mr. Martin, Timmins) negatived: Yeas, 29; nays, 59.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Shall clause 10 carry?

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wish to ask the minister a question on this clause which I think would possibly have been more correctly asked on an earlier clause, but I was unavoidably absent. My question has to do with paragraph (iii) of subclause (a) which deals with the maintenance of good human relations in industry. There are many unions in Canada representing thousands of workers which are not affiliated with the Canadian Labour Congress and whose members are making a considerable contribution to the Canadian economy in primary industries such as mining, fishing, transportation and construction. In view of the fact that there are many thousands of workers in the category I have mentioned, will there be an opportunity for representation on the council on behalf of unions not affiliated with the Canadian Labour Congress?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, ordinarily in appointing labour representatives to any organization established by the government, the representatives of the organized groups such as the Canadian Labour Congress, the National Federation of Trade Unions-that is the new name for the Canadian and Catholic Confederation of Labour-and in some cases where it is deemed advisable the legislative

committee of the railroad brotherhoods, are consulted. I realize there are unions that are particularly expert on some phases of the work that might be involved here. I believe representation from those people who might be affected, or who could be of some help, should be given consideration when appointments are made of the representatives of labour.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: I am very pleased to hear the minister say that, because that is the very point I had in mind. There are unions not affiliated with the congress whose officers and members have particular experience in a certain industry. Some of them are of long standing in Canada, and in my opinion some consideration should be given to these unions in representation on this council.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: In making a further comment on this may I say that I hope when something of that nature is done, there will be an understanding on the part of the Canadian Labour Congress and the federation of trade unions as to why it is being done, and I hope they will extend their co-operation.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: I hope so too.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I wonder if I may discuss with the minister the full intent of subparagraph 6, and whether or not it is a bit restrictive in its language. It reads:
(vi) the extension of industrial research programs in plants and in industries as a means of achieving greater productivity,
I think the implication here is that when it talks about extension, this would prohibit the fostering and promoting of the use of industrial research programs. When you speak of extension it seems to me to imply that there is such a thing in existence at the moment in all plants and industries. I believe that the words, "use and extension of" such programs might be better. This would allow the council to think in terms of discussing with any plant or any industry the institution of industrial research programs rather than their extension.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Many industries in this country have research programs of their own. For example, the pulp and paper research institute was set up by the pulp and paper industry. This productivity council, of course, will not be delving into research. I am certain, however, that if they felt it was necessary in a certain industry, and that the productivity of that industry would be increased through research, then the council might be in a position to advise that industry of this solution to the problem of gaining greater productivity in that particular industry. I feel that this productivity council will make full use of the facilities of the national research council
Productivity Council
in this respect, and possibly convey the information that may be derived from the national research council to a particular industry.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: As the minister has said, there are some industries which do not have any research programs. I wonder how this council could, as the bill says, promote the extension of research programs where none exist. How do you extend something that does not exist? If you were to put in the words "use and extension" it would make the clause much clearer.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: I explained a moment ago, I thought to the hon. member's satisfaction, that if in the opinion of the productivity council greater productivity could be brought about in an industry through research, no doubt the council would advise this industry that they avail themselves of research in some other area that is now in existence or set up their own research program. No doubt this council would give that sort of advice to that particular industry.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: I still do not see how you can extend something that does not exist. It is a matter of extension.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: I think the hon. member is playing on words. It is the extension of research that exists in one industry when it should also be undertaken in another industry; that is an extension.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I think the minister is playing on words, too, and he has had far more practice than I in this regard, belonging to the government that he does.
Let me look at another part of this clause, if I may. I think this is restrictive to the extent that it applies, in so far as research programs are concerned, only to industrial research programs, plants and industries. We are going to have a council representative of more than plants and industries. If you look back at clause 2 you will find there are to be five members chosen from the field of agriculture and other primary industries. Let us confine it to agriculture. How does this council get involved in the extension, to use the minister's play on words, of research programs in agriculture if the clause only makes reference to industrial research programs in plants and industries? Is it not restricted to that extent also?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: As a matter of fact the word "industries" covers the whole field. When you talk about the agricultural industry you are talking about the largest industry in this country.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
It may be that there are some people who will disagree with the minister in this regard. It does not say anywhere in

Productivity Council
the bill what an industry is. If it is the interpretation of the minister that you can extend an industrial research program to the agricultural industry, he is not only playing on words but he is being misled by words. In this connection I am reminded of an article in the Prince Rupert daily News, which gave a definition of politics. It says it is what makes you want to say sound like an answer to a question that was asked. This is obviously what we have got from the minister.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Get out of the gutter and get on with the bill.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Clause 10 sets out the general objects of this council. It reads:
The objects of the council are to promote and expedite continuing improvement in productive efficiency in the various aspects of Canadian economic activity, and without limiting the generality of the foregoing, the council may, in furtherance of its objects-
Before we can estimate just what gains we are making in productivity, it is necessary for us to know what the level of productivity is at a given time. What is our present output per man hour? When we come to inquire into that, we discover that there is a great lack of statistical information. I am told that there is a publication by Hood and Scott available from the Queen's printer which gives some figures, and I know that the Gordon commission presented some figures on productivity which were projected back, I understand, as far as 1926.
Recently the Senate committee on manpower and employment in their latest report, I think, dated December 8, has an appendix which for the first time lists the man hour productivity in various industries.
Apparently the difficulty with these figures is that there is no common denominator between them; hence they cannot be used for accurate comparisons. On December 13 the Prime Minister put on Hansard some figures which he attributed to Dr. Eugene Forsey, the research director of the Canadian Labour Congress. I take issue with some of the figures given by Dr. Forsey, because I think they are apt to mislead us as to what our real gain in productivity actually is. At the bottom of page 748 of Hansard Dr. Forsey is quoted in the following words:
In 1946, the number with jobs in manufacturing was about 1,222,000. Last year, it was 1,502,000 ... or an increase of 23 per cent.
The Prime Minister then went on to elaborate as follows:
Then he says-
That is Dr. Forsey.
-that while there was an increase in manufacturing employment of about 23 per cent during that period, the gain in manufacturing production was about 75 per cent.

A little further on he again quotes Dr. Forsey in these words:
From 1947 to 1959 manufacturing production rose almost 60 per cent; manufacturing jobs rose only about 19 per cent.
What I want to point out is that a contrast of that kind does not give us an accurate picture of what our gain in productivity actually is. In April of 1959 I put on Hansard some figures which I should like to quote at the present time. As I stated on Wednesday evening, we can get a rough idea of our productivity as a nation if we take our gross national product in constant dollars and divide it by the average labour force. In 1954 our gross national product in constant dollars was $20,186 million and our average labour force was 5.493 million. If we divide the gross national product by the labour force we get a figure of 370. If we go on to 1958 we find that the gross national product in constant dollars in 1958 was $23,704 million while the average labour force was 6.127 million. If we divide the latter figure into the former one we get a comparable quotient of 387. That computation works out to a gain of about 5 per cent in four years or an over-all yearly gain of about 1J per cent in productivity for the nation as a whole.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Order. Will the hon. member explain how he can relate his remarks to clause 10 of the bill which is under consideration?

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman. I thought I had done so at the beginning of my remarks, when I said that clause 10 sets forth that a general objective of this council is to promote and expedite continuing improvement in productive efficiency in the various aspects of Canadian economic activity. I was saying that if we are to promote improvement in our efficiency we must know what our starting point is, or in other words we must know what our productivity figure or index is at the present time. That is the purpose of this discussion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Even if clause 10 describes the objectives and powers of the council and therefore deals with the purposes of the bill, we should now discuss the terms of clause 10 and it seems to me that this discussion must be more strictly relevant to the wording and substance of clause 10 than to the purposes which are therein referred to.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am dealing directly with the purpose of clause 10, which is the purpose of council as set out under this clause. What I am going on to point out is this. After stating the general objectives', clause 10 goes

on to enumerate a number of specific objectives, one of which is contained in subparagraph (vi) which reads as follows:
(vi) the extension of industrial research programs-[DOT]
I should like to point out that it is equally necessary to promote a statistical research program. I know that a great deal of statistical research is being carried out in various departments at the present time. The Department of Trade and Commerce has a statistical branch. The bureau of statistics has a statistical branch. I think there is another one in the Department of Labour. I am not suggesting that the council should undertake a program which would duplicate what is already being done. Rather I am suggesting that there should be some agency to coordinate this work in such a way that we shall have a figure which will enable us as a nation to measure our progress in technical efficiency and will also enable one industry to compare its progress with the progress that is being made in other industries. We have not such a figure at the present time, and I think it is essential that we should have one.
I would be the first to admit that it is not easy to get a figure that will have great accuracy because there are many factors which vary from one industry to the other. For example, as has been pointed out by many hon. members, productivity is in large measure geared to our markets, and when markets begin to decline there is a tendency for a decline in productivity corresponding with the fall in the market. That factor varies from one industry to the other, and it is a factor which would affect the index figure. In addition, a firm might be faced with the choice of laying off people or of working to a limited capacity, and they may not be able to obtain full efficiency with part of their plant lying idle. Then there are others who would be faced with a choice between the cost of closing down and reopening as compared with the cost of carrying their staff while not fully employed. These are all factors that vary and there is a need for somebody to work out a common denominator that will permit an adjustment to be made in the calculation of productivity figures which will at least give us an approximate idea of how we are doing with regard to our gain in technical efficiency. For that reason I move:
That paragraph (a) of clause 10 be amended by deleting the word "and" at the end of line 24 and adding the following:
(viii) The promotion and co-ordination of statistical research into man hour productivity on a basis that will be comparable for all industries.
Productivity Council

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: I think I should make some observations on this proposed amendment. At the present time a great deal of information is available on production by industries through the dominion bureau of statistics, and we also have a good deal of information available in the Department of Labour concerning manpower. The dominion bureau of statistics has a special section which deals with productivity measurement, and this section will be able to supply information to the council which should be helpful. The job of this council will be to help to improve productivity, not to measure it. It will have at its disposal all the information which is available, and I doubt whether any further information could be amassed as a result of an amendment of the type proposed here.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: The point is this. How do you know you are improving productivity if you have no means of measuring it?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: We have.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Can the minister tell me what our output per man hour is at the present time as a nation?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
If the hon. member had told me he wanted that information I think I should have been able to provide it for him.
Amendment (Mr. Carter) negatived: Yeas, 20; nays, 34.

I have read through the whole of this bill, though somewhat hurriedly, and I may be mistaken in this statement; but as far as I can observe the word "employment" and the word "unemployment" do not occur anywhere in the bill, except that the word "employment" is used once in the preamble. In the body of the bill, the operative part, there seems to have been an oversight, and nowhere is there any reference to employment or unemployment. Since we are told this measure is part of the government's plan to promote employment and cure unemployment, it seems to me there is a very simple way of remedying the omission. I do not intend to make a long speech about it. I am just going to move an amendment. I move:
That clause 10 be amended by inserting in line 6 on page 3 after the word "efficiency" the words "and employment".
The effect of this amendment would be to make the clause read:
The objects of the council are to promote and expedite continuing improvement in productive efficiency and employment in the various aspects of Canadian economic activity-
I cannot imagine that the government will not welcome this rescue operation on the part of the opposition.
