speechtext:
Reading through the debates it is clear, I think, that the concept which the Minister of Labour had with regard to this bill was one which would be shared more widely on this side of the house than by most of his colleagues, at least by those of his colleagues in the government who have spoken on the measure.
As far as the Prime Minister or the Minister of Trade and Commerce were concerned, this bill was intended to deal primarily with the purposes and objects as stated in clause 10. But the Minister of Labour, recognizing the importance of this problem, did say at one point, in the only clear and succinct statement which has been made by the minister yet on this measure, that it was also intended to deal with unemployment. Indeed, we have been led to believe that one of the reasons we are here at this time of the year is to give the government power to bring in more vigorous methods of dealing with unemployment.
I believe that of all the amendments introduced by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate in the course of his brilliant parliamentary career, none has had as great and as constructive a purpose as the amendment in his name now standing before us. The hon. gentleman has pointed out that all throughout this bill there has been, for some reason or other, a reluctance on the part of

the administration to recognize the existence of either employment or unemployment. Certainly nothing in the operational part of the bill by implication or directly has any reference to the problem of unemployment or employment. The hon. member for one of the eastern townships who spoke a while ago suddenly thought he had found an unusual bit of information for the committee when he observed that there was reference in the second line of the preamble to the word "employment", and of course the hon. member's chagrin was great when he was reminded that that was one of the very points made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
It is worth while looking at the preamble again:
Whereas in order to provide expanding opportunities for increased employment and trade and rising national standards of living, it is in the national interest to promote and expedite continuing improvement in productive efficiency in the various aspects of Canadian economic activity-
That is the only reference in this bill to the most serious problem that confronts us in Canada at this time, certainly on the domestic level; yet there is a refusal on the part of the government to carry into the operational part of the bill what is stated so piously in the preamble.
If the word "employment" is not to be included in clause 10, as is proposed in the amendment of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, then why should it be in the preamble? I should certainly want it to be in the preamble in any event so we would at least have that degree of recognition by this government in this bill of the seriousness of the need for employment. What possible reason can the government give for this exclusion? What possible reason can the Minister of Labour in particular give for not including a reference of this nature in the measure? He is the one minister who in the statements he has made about this bill has said it is intended to deal with employment. He is confident it will deal with it in the short term, because the minister said that by next July, six months hence, we would have some indication of the effect of this bill on employment conditions.
I suggest that if the government persists in refusing to accept this amendment it only justifies the contention we have been making that this measure and its companion measures, all of them introduced at a time when we unanimously agreed to dispense with the debate on the speech from the throne, are intended not to provide the government with methods to cure unemployment or to provide a mitigation of unemployment but to provide the government with an excuse for not dealing with unemployment, so that later on hon. gentlemen opposite can piously refer to these

great measures passed in the early part of this session when we unanimously agreed to postpone our normal discussions in order to deal with these important emergency measures.
What is emergent about this, unless there is a recognition of the actual fact of heavy unemployment in this country? There were
425,000	unemployed people in Canada as of yesterday, a figure that is growing day by day and month by month. All this government does is bring forward bills that look impressive in form but that are really merely facades for the government to enable hon. gentlemen opposite to make strong speeches of achievement later on, as they will certainly do and as the Prime Minister assuredly will do when he talks about having fulfilled all of his promises. He will say that the government brought in a bill to provide for a productivity council that will seriously affect the problem of unemployment, but he will not tell the committee or the country that the government through the Minister of Labour has refused to accept, in the statement of the objects of the council, reference to employment in the way suggested by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
In spite of the criticism I have levelled and will continue to level against his administration, I believe the Minister of Labour is sincere in the job he has undertaken. But I say he does not do himself justice when, as Minister of Labour, he does not accept this amendment which will clearly establish that one of the functions of this council is not only to produce efficiency but also, at least in the long term, to do something about employment.
The reluctance of the government to accept this amendment is the most demonstrative proof we have had of the fact that the government, in spite of the propaganda it has used during the past three or four weeks, is not disposed to seriously tackle the problem of unemployment in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, there are two phrases in clause 11 to which I should like to address myself for a moment or two. First I should like to refer to subclause (a) which reads as follows:
Subject to the approval of the governor in council, make bylaws regulating its proceedings and generally for the conduct of its activities, including the establishment of regional offices.
In other words, the bill gives the council the authority to make its own bylaws and regulations. That is a provision that has been used over the years in legislation creating a body of this kind. Provision is made that the body shall have the right to make its own bylaws in order to administer its affairs. However, there is one aspect of such bylaws or regulations to which I am certainly opposed. We frequently find in such regulations that it is provided that there shall be no appeal from any decision made by the body in question.
I simply make this observation and hope the minister is familiar with the fact that there is a tendency to make such a regulation providing that there shall be no appeal from any decision of the body or council. Having in mind the fact that the bill of rights is now law and also the fact that in the last two years a number of great legal and parliamentary authorities have taken the position that to give a body created by statute the authority to be final in its decisions creates a form of supreme court, I simply ask the minister to take cognizance of that tendency at the present time.
This council is to be given the power to make regulations for its own administration but I should like the minister to see to it that the council does not obtain such authority, as has happened sometimes in the past, and I hope any such authority now exercised will be minimized as time goes on. I would ask the minister to see that in this case there is nothing in the regulations to provide that the council shall have the last word without any appeal to the courts, thus making the council a sort of supreme court of Canada. This is a dangerous trend. I should like to

appeal to the minister to see to it that the council does not obtain the same authority as the Supreme Court of Canada.
With respect to subclauses (b) and (c), I should like to draw the minister's attention to this point. Under subclause (b) the council may acquire by purchase, lease, gift, donation, bequest or otherwise. How can the council acquire otherwise that which it seeks to acquire? Therefore, I should like the minister to tell us what is meant by the use of the word "otherwise". The same word also appears in subclause (c) where it is provided that the council may expend moneys received by it through the conduct of its operations or by gift, donation, bequest or otherwise.
Although I am not now addressing myself to clause 16, I should like to point out that the word "otherwise" is not used although we And there a similar phrase. This is not simply a matter of semantics. The inclusion of the word "otherwise" means nothing unless it is intended to cover something about which we cannot be told. If it is intended to cover something about which we are not to know, then why is the word "otherwise" included? Under paragraphs (b) and (c) every possible means of acquiring property have already been specified, such as lease, gift, donation, bequest, so what does the word "otherwise" cover?

speechtext: Just on that same subject, if I may add a word. Clause 11 sets out many modes by which the council may acquire property, while clause 16 simply limits the mode to three cases, donations, gifts or bequests. If the hon. gentleman will consider that for an. instant he will find that these three words refer, in effect, to donations and, in such case, there is provision for appropriation by the council of an amount equal to such donations. In clause 11 we are dealing with the different methods by which the council may acquire property and it would be outlandish to try to specify every means. It is for this reason that in clause 11 the word "otherwise" is included, whereas in clause 16 the word "otherwise" is not included. Mr. Dorion Mr. Chairman, I think my hon. colleague has often had occasion to see this word in various statutes, where it is obviously used to remove any possibility of impediments to the acquisition of needed property. It should be noted here that clause 11 deals with the objects and powers of the council. Indeed, it reads as follows:
In addition to the general powers conferred upon or vested in the council by this act the council may,
b) acquire by purchase, lease, gift, donation, bequest or otherwise-
There might be other methods of acquiring, which are unprovided for here and which might perhaps be an obstacle to the acquiring or renting; that accounts for the use here of this word which, by the way, occurs in many statutes of similar nature. I cannot see how the word might constitute an obstacle or an objection, particularly in the light of paragraph (c), which reads as follows:
-expend any moneys appropriated by parliament for the work of the council or received by the council through the conduct of its operations or by gift, donation, bequest or otherwise.

Of course, parliament retains a very large measure of control over the operations of the council, or rather the department will be kept informed of the council's activity, and I fail to see how the word "otherwise" could be a serious objection to this clause.
Of course, if I strained my imagination a little, I might find an example that would give full satisfaction to my hon. colleague. None occurs to me at the moment, but I am sure that with a bit of thought one could find a case where the word would apply; in fact, if the word were left out of the bill, the omission might, at a given time, hinder the proper operation of the council.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I acknowledge your appreciation of the traditions of the house and the ready recognition of the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) of the force of those traditions.
We are now about to deal with the final procedural arrangements in connection with the government's policy to seek to resolve unemployment in Canada. I am sure that on third reading we would not want to be denied the opportunity of expressing our deep regret at what the government has brought forward in this attempt to provide some solution for what unfortunately continues to be the foremost domestic problem in our country. That was highlighted yesterday by the latest release of figures on unemployment which indicates an increasingly serious situation in that regard, more serious than in the comparable period in the previous year. I can only say that the parade of the government's program in this session is not one that gives anyone any justification for believing that the government finally, after three years of prodding, has embarked on a program capable of meeting the situation.
It is true that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) said before we were called together, that this session was not to be regarded as meeting in an emergency; that it was not to be regarded as being anything other than an attempt to provide for hon. members an opportunity to be free of responsibility in this chamber during the summer months. But undoubtedly, the impression was created by the Prime Minister in his speech last night and in the speech he made to the people of Canada on September 21 that the government did regard unemployment as a serious problem and that it had a program designed to meet that problem. Undoubtedly, in regard to the four pieces of legislation, of which this is the last one, namely that dealing with small loans, vocational training and technical assistance, the housing legislation and the legislation setting up the productivity council, an endeavour will be made to create the impression by the administration and by its spokesmen that in these four measures the government has brought forward a vigorous, comprehensive program to attack unemployment.
Let there be no doubt about this. Legislation that the government has brought forward, with the exception of that brought
[The Acting Speaker.]
forward by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker), does not in any serious way provide any solution at the present time for what is a serious problem in our country, more serious than in any other country in the western world, notwithstanding the statement of the Prime Minister two nights ago that this problem was parallelled by the situation in the United States. I have no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that notwithstanding these statements, when this measure is passed the government, through its propaganda agencies, through its spokesmen over the television, on the radio and in the favoured press, will seek to convey to the Canadian people, and particularly to the unemployed of this country, that it has brought forward legislation designed to deal with this current situation of unemployment.
Today we were told by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) that this measure to set up a productivity council was not intended as a solution to unemployment, notwithstanding his statement of the other day. Likewise we have the statement of the Prime Minister, who dodged the question of unemployment completely in his peregrination two days ago. I have no doubt that once this bill becomes law the Prime Minister and his colleagues will go from one end of this country to the other trying to establish in the public mind that they have dealt with unemployment by these four legislative acts.
I am sure the Prime Minister, when he talks about the productivity council, will not make to the Canadian people the kind of speech he made last night, or the speech he made the day before; he will talk about the productivity council as one of the effective instruments designed by this government, following a consultation with labour, management and agriculture, to try to provide a solution to the problem of unemployment. He will do the same with regard to the small loans legislation and the vocational training legislation. But let this be clear. Notwithstanding what will be said about this measure by the government supporters, this particular bill-and it is true of its companion bills on small loans, vocational training and technical assistance-does not in any substantial or serious way provide any solution to the problem of unemployment which stares this government in the face and confronts the people of Canada at this time.
But that is not the impression the Prime Minister created before we came here, as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) pointed out so effectively this afternoon. When the Prime Minister spoke to the people of Canada on the "Nation's Business" on September 21 he did not hesitate to acknowledge that at long

last that there was a serious problem of unemployment. He could not help but face the situation because of the unprecedented character of unemployment in the month of September last in comparison with the same month in other years. It is understandable why, in the closing remarks of that speech, when speaking on unemployment, as he did all the way through, he should have concluded, in part, with these words, which are found on page 8 of the release given out by the Prime Minister's office:
More must and will be done. Our plans are already made and will be presented in detail to the next session of parliament. Naturally I cannot say what these plans are in those matters which require the approval of parliament,-
But we now have those plans; we now know what they are. I ask the Prime Minister, does he really believe, now that the plans have been substantially exposed and presented in detail at this session of parliament, that we have been presented with the kind of solution which is designed to provide and capable of providing, not a year from now, not 10 years from now, but now, some mitigation of this problem of unemployment?
The Prime Minister created the impression that there can be no doubt that the government had plans. Not only did the government have plans but it was prepared to sit down and listen to the representatives of labour, management, agriculture and the universities, and then to get their-

speechtext: Didn't he?

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, he did, for one day. I am going to deal with that in a minute. Yes, he did, and it was at the end of that conference, a conference, mind you, that lasted one day-as though there could be a satisfactory discussion between the various partners of industry, between the various segments of the Canadian economy in regard to unemployment in one day; I do not know how many organizations there were but I believe there were at least 25 which made representations of one sort or another-all of this took place in one day, and at the end of that day the Prime Minister announced the government's decision to bring in the productivity council, which is the soul and the substance of this particular bill.
Obviously, this was not the result of the suggestions by the parties to the conference. This had already been in the minds of the government; undoubtedly, this was already part of the plans which the Prime Minister referred to when he spoke to the Canadian people on September 21 last. The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Brunsden) said, "Did he not have a conference"? My answer is of course he had a conference.
Productivity Council
But there are two points to make in connection with that intervention. We have urged the government for three years to call a conference of representatives of labour, management, agriculture, universities and other interested parties in this country. We have been asking the government to do that very thing. We were told session after session by the Minister of Labour and perhaps by the Prime Minister, although I do not remember, that this government was elected to do a job and that they did not propose to dodge that responsibility. That was the answer given to me and to other hon. gentlemen in this party when we proposed that a conference should be called to discuss ways and means of arriving at a co-operative method for resolving or mitigating the problem of unemployment.
Only last April the Minister of Labour made a speech in Gananoque in which finally he seemed to acknowledge the desirability of such a conference. I put a question to the Minister of Labour in which I asked: "Are we to take this speech in Gananoque as meaning that the government has accepted our suggestion that there should be a conference?" The Minister of Labour dodged the question. He refused to indicate whether or not the government intended to call such a conference.
But the record is clear. Right from the very first session of the present parliament this government was urged to call such a conference and it did so only this fall after a continuous repetition of statistics indicating how serious the problem of unemployment in Canada is. So what the government was doing in that conference, which lasted only a day and should have taken many days of serious discussion, back and forth, to ascertain what the views of the parties concerned really were, was to accept belatedly a proposal that had been put forward by the Liberal opposition on no less than five different occasions during the course of the present parliament.
We have at long last in the statement of the Prime Minister on September 21, a recognition that this problem is a serious one, but in recognizing that it is serious the Prime Minister disclaims that this is a responsibility of the federal government. This, he says, and I think rightly, is a responsibility that must be shared by all levels of government. But that is not what the right hon. gentleman said when he confronted the Canadian people in the elections of 1957 and 1958. He said, "We will resolve this problem; this is a federal responsibility". He did not then talk about the responsibility as one that should be shared by the provinces, nor did the Minister of Labour as a private member of the house when, sitting in the opposition, who*

Productivity Council
said that this was a responsibility of the federal government. He criticized the former administration for seeking to place the responsibility on the provinces as well.
What does the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees), that gentleman who has been transferred from one department to another and who is absent from the house on business outside the country, now say about the responsibility of the federal government with regard to unemployment? We will not forget the speeches he made when he was in the opposition. He says now that this is not a responsibility of the federal government but rather a responsibility of the Canadian people. That is what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said in the month of September when he too was confronted with the official statistics of rising unemployment in Canada. That is not the position that hon. gentlemen opposite took when in 1957, they went before the Canadian people and complained about government inaction in the field of social and economic welfare. That is not the position that the government took at the beginning of the present parliament.
But now what do we have presented to us? In the third year of this parliament, when unemployment continues to be so serious as to cause the greatest concern, what do we have from a government that was going to resolve this problem as it had never been resolved before? Four measures that are nothing more than facades, pretentions at achievement, nothing more.

speechtext: How did you vote?

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL

speechtext:
The small loans legislation does not add one bit to the solution or alleviation of unemployment. The housing legislation is the only measure which we hope and recognize is designed to bring some relief in that regard. Certainly the vocational training program is good in principle but long term in effect and it is not going to put one person to work immediately. It is not designed even to provide ad hoc training for men and women who can take advantage of such instruction and thereby receive employment now, not six months, not a year, not two years from now.
Then we have the productivity council bill. These three pieces of legislation, excluding the housing act amendments, represent thus far the government's so called vigorous approach to solving the problem of unemployment. One can only say that the result is disappointing. The result does not represent a vigorous, dynamic approach on the part of the administration to the solution of this problem and the reason for that is that

the government has waited too late. The government has come forward too late. If it had listened to the Liberal opposition-

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.

speechtext: You would have done nothing.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I say now that if the Prime Minister had listened to what we said in the fall of 1958, if he had established an advisory council, if he had enlisted the assistance of those who by training could advise the government, not determine their policy but advise the government, the government would not now be portrayed, as it is from one end of Canada to the other, as a do-nothing government in the matter of unemployment. That is the fact. The government hoped by taking a relaxed course, by letting this problem run its course, that time would take care of the problem but time has caught up with the right hon. gentleman and his colleagues. Time is not taking care of the problem. The problem is growing more and more serious.
When we think that the Minister of Labour, speaking for the government, refused this house the right to a parliamentary committee two years ago to examine the problem of unemployment, so that we could have experts come before such a committee to assess the nature of the problem and to provide solutions, when we think that the elected representatives of the people in this house are denied a privilege accorded to members in another chamber, the recollection of this situation only points up the bankruptcy of ideas on the part of the government with respect to this matter.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL

speechtext: My friend the Prime Minister always resorts to precedent. What the Prime Minister forgets is this: Whatever may have been the situation in the past we are now confronted in this country with a very serious problem and the government should address itself to that problem. They should not seek refuge in mistakes or in history. They should seek refuge in courageous attempts to deal with the problem and not to dodge it as the present government seeks to dodge most questions.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Then do not waste so much time talking against it.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I do so because I want to bring home to the government that they have no unemployment policy. I should have thought a C.C.F. member would be the first to support what I am seeking to do at this moment. Why should the Liberal party have imposed on it the responsibility, the sole responsibility, of exposing the weaknesses of the government unemployment policy? We shall vote for this bill not because we regard this as a solution to the problem of unemployment but because this bill may contain, in the long term, some benefit for the people of Canada. Having said that, I do not want the government to be under any misapprehension as to what we think of the shortcomings of this bill.
The Prime Minister, who is now making notes, can get up afterwards and talk all he wants; he can use these indirections, these diversions instead of addressing himself to the problem of unemployment. I know that he will say the hon. member for Essex East, having so seriously criticized us, nevertheless made a big mistake when he announced he was going to vote for the bill. That is the kind of argument which the Prime Minister makes at all times. I am saying to the Prime Minister, you were elected to do a job; you promised to do something about unemployment. I am saying here, as the representative
Productivity Council
of thousands and thousands of men out of work in my constituency, this government has dodged its responsibility and is doing that now in the matter of unemployment.
Is there any doubt, Mr. Speaker, that what I am saying is the case? The Prime Minister spoke on this bill. He was concerned with the relationship of the council to unemployment but he spoke about everything else but unemployment. I have examined the speech the Prime Minister made the other night, and there was no reference whatever to the problem of unemployment. Is this bill designed to assist the unemployed or is it not? I want to examine this aspect of the problem. We have had two interesting statements by the Minister of Labour, one this afternoon and the other when he spoke on this bill two days ago. The Minister of of Labour said, as recorded at page 781 of Hansard for this session:
The ultimate and most important job of the productivity council will be, if automation is resorted to in an industry in order to accelerate productivity, to recommend the retraining of the people who are displaced so that they may be best fitted into some other useful employment in our labour force.
In that statement, at any rate, the Minister of Labour recognized the problem of unemployment. He did recognize that, and in his judgment this particular bill could presumably bring about some mitigation of the current problem. But that is not what the Prime Minister said. The Prime Minister said nothing whatever about this bill in terms of providing a remedy for unemployment. The reason I mention what the Prime Minister said was so that we will have on the record this statement, which I believe to be valid, because I have no doubt that in the months to come the Prime Minister will hold this bill up as one of the instruments by which the government dealt with the problem of unemployment, not only in the long term but in the short term. The Prime Minister is a master at this kind of innocent deception, a kind of innocent deception that in the past has had its influence and has made its impression on the electorate. We shall see whether that success of the Prime Minister shall continue in the light of this dismal record of failure on the part of the government to act.
Today the Minister of Labour made another statement. I took down his words as he replied to a question put by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. The Minister of Labour said that the effect of this amendment-that is the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate- would be that the council would be dealing

Productivity Council
directly with the employment or unemployment factor and that is not to be the case. There we have an admission from the Minister of Labour that is consistent with the declaration of the Prime Minister that this particular bill is not to be regarded as dealing directly with the problem of unemployment. The Minister of Labour and the Prime Minister are in agreement on this, and we have-

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: I rise on a question of personal privilege, if I may. The hon. member for Essex East, of course, is the sort of person who takes words out of context. If he would go on and state what followed after that he would find, as nearly as I can recall from memory, that I said this council will bring about efficiency and productivity of industry and, consequently, employment will flow from that.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Whatever the Minister of Labour says, I accept. I am simply pointing out what he did say, and I took his words down directly. I ask hon. members to compare those words with what the Prime Minister said, and to compare them particularly with the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce who introduced this measure several days ago. So far as the Minister of Trade and Commerce was concerned this bill was not designed in any way to do other than what was done under a similar measure in the United Kingdom. It was part of his great campaign to increase production, as though merely increasing production was the corollary of increasing employment. The hon. member for Brome-Mis-sisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) said that by merely providing for increased productivity you were providing at the same time for increased employment. He forgets that is not true. He forgets that the effects of automation in industry have been otherwise. He fails to point out that in agriculture over the last 10 years production has almost doubled but the reduction in employment in the agricultural industry has been about 25 per cent. There are about 25 per cent less people now working in agriculture, in spite of the great increase in production.
It is clear, whatever may be said by hon. members hereafter, there is agreement between the Prime Minister, the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Trade and Commerce that this measure is not designed to provide a cure for unemployment. That is not what the Prime Minister said on September 21; that is not the statement the Prime Minister gave when he conferred with representatives of labour and other segments of the population in this city a few weeks ago.

I am sure, knowing the hon. gentleman as I do, that will not be the kind of statement he will give to the Canadian people when he seeks to impress on the people what his government has sought to do to live up to the assurances that he gave to the Canadian people during the course of the last federal election campaign.
Here is an interesting statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, which is to be found at page 566 of Hansard for this session:
The national council should act as a policy making body and should assist in the establishment of regional and industry productivity committees. Its chief objective should be to develop and maintain in the various and changing circumstances of industrial life a positive attitude of mind in industry, among both management and labour, respecting industrial efficiency.
It is to be a policy making body. It is not to be merely one to make recommendations. Yet in the absence of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Labour refused to accept an amendment that would give the council the authority and the power to make recommendations to the executive. The amendment introduced by the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) called for the council to be given explicit power to make recommendations to the executive-not to formulate policy but merely to make recommendations-and this power was denied, although the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that the council should act as a policy making body.
What was the reply of the Minister of Labour year after year, session after session, when we urged upon the government the setting up of a national advisory council? The Minister of Labour said that the formulation of policy must be left to the administration and must not be left to any outside or subsidiary body. He said that was why they could not accept the Liberal proposal for a national advisory council on unemployment and automation. That is what the Minister of Labour said during the course of previous sesions of parliament. Yet his colleague in introducing this measure took the very opposite position and said that this was to be a bill providing for a council that would have the power of formulating policy in the matters that parliament would allocate to it.
This matter is one which we feel must be thoroughly discussed and thoroughly understood in its proper context so that there will be no misunderstanding in the future as to what the government's intentions are and so that there will be no misunderstanding about this measure not really being part of a vigorous program designed to solve the problem of unemployment.

This measure, like its companion measure, is designed to deal with this situation indirectly and in the long term. No effort is made in any of the measures proposed by the government to assess the problem immediately, or to examine the nature of the problem in distressed areas. There is no sense of urgency such as that which we find in the other place in the studies that are being made there. We had here yesterday a delegation of unemployed from Windsor. I listened to the government reply or response to the representations that were made. I am sure I do not take unfair advantage, in saying that the government did not reflect a determination or a capacity to act, or did not indicate that it had a program designed to meet the particular situation, let alone the national picture. This government has yet to bring to this house any report that will tell us what is the nature of unemployment in the particular areas that are especially depressed. I am thinking of areas like my own, the maritime provinces, the city of Levis and so on.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL

speechtext: And Port Arthur.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, and Port Arthur and other cities. This government should certainly have approached this problem in the way in which we urged it to approach it and in the way in which the other place is gradually developing an approach to the solution of this problem. This government has won and deserved the indictment of the Canadian people and of this house for its failure adequately to confront this problem. Of that fact there can be no doubt. When one examines what is being attempted by the new president of the United States, by the legislative program that is now being forecast, one finds that an attempt will be made in that country to deal with the situations as they exist in particular communities. That is what is being done by an administration that has not yet taken office as compared with the results of this administration which has been in office since March, 1958 and particularly by a government that gave such great assurances to the Canadian people.
There can be no doubt that this problem is one that cries for the kind of solution that we can give. It is a problem that touches the very soul of our society. Unless it is met forthrightly and courageously by the government, regardless of whether or not it runs across the traditional concepts of our society, it will do more harm to our free society than will anything else. I call on this government in these late hours to recognize that it has a responsibility which it is not discharging. In order to bring this matter more forcefully to the attention of the government and
Productivity Council
that of the Canadian people I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith):
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"Bill C-52 be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of amending clause 10 to include the promotion of employment as one of the specific objects of the council."
It is not too late for this government to take action that will be effective.

Then I will place the amendment before the house. Mr. Martin (Essex East) seconded by Mr. Mcllraith moved:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"Bill No. C-52 be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of amending clause 10 to include the promotion of employment as one of the specific objects of the council."

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
As I began to say, before the house rose at six o'clock I listened with a great deal of interest to what is becoming known as the usual ranting and raving of the hon. member for Essex East on his favourite subject, using the same speech as he so often uses, with its tossed salad type of verbiage. The hon. member said that this government took three years before it brought about any conference on unemployment in this country. His memory is short. If he thinks

Productivity Council
back to July, 1958 he will recall that I called a conference here in Ottawa. Representatives of labour, agriculture, industry and other important segments of our economy gathered here to discuss the problem of unemployment at that time. As a result of that conference the municipal winter works program was inaugurated that fall, and the success of that program has continued ever since that time.
The hon. member talked about the unemployment situation in Canada and said it is not right to compare it with the situation in any other country on the North American continent. Let me inform him that in the United States at this moment there is something like 6.4 per cent of the labour force unemployed-well over four million people-[DOT] and most certainly we have a relationship with that country across the border, and whatever happens in the United States is bound to affect our economy.
1 would point out also that there are always two sides to the picture and we must not forget this positive aspect of our economy, namely that there are more people employed now than ever before in the history of this country on a month to month basis. As to a comparison between November of 1960 and November of 1959, I may say there are some
99,000	more people employed in this country this year than there were last year.
It depends on the viewpoint one takes. There is always a positive and a negative side to a question. We have not said we do not recognize the serious situation presented by unemployment, and this is borne out by the measures which this government has taken since we came to office in 1957 and 1958. This session certainly shows that this government is well aware of the current situation, because each and every measure which has been brought before the house has been designed for the sole purpose of providing employment and bolstering the economy of this country.
The hon. member for Essex East in presenting his amendment finds himself in his usual position of watching the parade go by and then having to run to catch up with it. I remember reading a report of a debate in the thirties when the hon. member was on the government side of the house. It was a debate on unemployment in this chamber and when one of the members from Toronto, Mr. Massey, was speaking, the hon. member for Essex East said: Let us get this over; I have a train to catch. The hon. member has been catching trains ever since; he has been in a hurry ever since.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: I always got there.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
You left the unemployment debate to catch that train, too.
The hon. gentleman talks about unemployment in Windsor. Let me say that the figures show that ever since he was elected to be a member of parliament for Windsor, that is when unemployment started in that city. What did the hon. gentleman say in 1954 when Ford was moving to Oakville? Did he raise his voice and say they should not undermine the industrial position of that city?

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: The minister has asked me a question. He asked me what I did.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I can answer the question because I know the facts. Anyway the hon. member for Essex East is not happy about the present bill. He is not happy about the other bills that have been brought before the house, either. He is not happy with any of the measures which the government has evolved in order to maintain a stable economy and provide employment. Let me say this: I have a strong suspicion that there will be no satisfying the hon. member for Essex East, no matter what this government does. I think he is resolved at all costs to maintain his position of not being satisfied with anything. I think the hon. member has in his make-up a sort of gloating, gleeful personality which seems to gloat at any undermining of our economy because, as has been said by one of the hon. member's friends who is preparing to be a candidate for the Liberal party, the only way the Liberal party can assume power again is through a depression in this country.
In any event, the attitude of the hon. member for Essex East is completely negative, destructive and obstructionist. Let me advise him that he would go a lot further in carrying out the role of a reasonable and constructive member of the opposition if, from time to time at least, he could bring himself to admit that some of the things the government is doing have some prospect of being useful and successful. I honestly believe that in his heart the hon. member realizes that this government has been endeavouring to do everything in its power to help the economic situation. If not, why does the hon. member vote for these measures? Why does he place on them his stamp of approval by voting for them after spending so much time rehashing the same old speech he gives in this house from time to time?

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: It is puny, but one more step; and late, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
One of the measures recently approved by this house was the housing measure. The hon. member for Essex East

said it was a good measure but that he had some grave doubts about its effectiveness. Let me assure the hon. gentleman that he should' not have had any doubts about it because action in this field is already taking place. Let me refer to the following article in this evening's issue of the Ottawa Citizen:
Ottawa Seeks Sewage Loan-$10 Million.
Ottawa will seek a loan of $10 million from the federal government to expedite completion of a $20 million sewage disposal project.
Mayor Nelms said the move is to take advantage of new federal legislation under which loans amounting to two-thirds of the total cost for sewage disposal projects can be secured, and under which 25 per cent of the total cost of works finished by March, 1963, will be rebated.
"This will save Ottawa approximately $2,500,000," the mayor emphasized.
Here is an example of direct action that has been taken as a result of the direct and immediate action taken by this government. A recent issue of the Ottawa Citizen carried an article under the headline "Plan 350 Homes for Low Incomes" which reads in part as follows:
A plan to provide low cost housing for people in the low income brackets was submitted to board of control by Robert Campeau, president of Campeau Construction Company Limited.
Mr. Campeau told the board he planned the construction of 350 housing units on the old Arkell farm lying between Pinecrest and the Walkley roads south of the Queensway.
Mr. Campeau is reported as having said:
"It has been said private enterprises would not provide low cost housing for people in the low income brackets," Mr. Campeau said. "Now because of the favourable financing provided by the federal government, through C.M.H.C., we are able to do, on terms comparable with city schemes for low rental, full recovery projects."
He said he already had 200 applications for the low cost housing. The salary range for people applying is from $3,800 to $4,500, he advised the board.
He added that the provision of services would be carried by the subdivider in relation to all facilities save a trunk sewer.
There is another indication of what is happening as a result of the legislation this government introduced.
Let us take a look at what is being done in the field of vocational and technical schools. As soon as third reading was given to the bill in this house the government of Ontario announced a $8 million program to be started immediately under this plan.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: They had that in mind before, and the minister knows it. It was in the speech from the throne.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
That, Mr. Speaker, is an answer to the hon. member for Essex East who said that the legislation concerning vocational training and technical schools would not bring immediate results in the form of jobs.
Productivity Council

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: May I direct a question to the minister? Is it not a fact that the $8 million referred to is half the quota until March 31, 1967 according to the minister's own words the other day?

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman looking for another headline?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
It amounts to a great deal more than $8 million. It is going to be a very large program undertaken by all the provinces across this country amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars as a result of this legislation. That is only a start. I say that all the measures we have been bringing forward are already having their effects. The hon. member for Essex East has singled out only four measures. He did not even have the patience to wait to see the whole program before condemning it. As a matter of fact he is condemning the program in advance.
In his attitude the hon. member for Essex East reminds me somewhat of a small boy at Christmas time who rushes in, tears all the wrapping off the presents and then sets up a howl that what was in the boxes was not what he wanted. I submit the simple truth is that the hon. member did not get his little red wagon, Mr. Speaker. In the case of the hon. gentleman he cannot even wait until Christmas but has to start howling even before the packages are unwrapped. I say that is not a responsible attitude.
Let us now look at the hon. member's amendment. I submit this is not a serious amendment. In the first place the inclusion of the phrase which the hon. member so strenuously urges is unnecessary as I pointed out at the committee stage. I attempted to make it clear that the purpose of this bill is set out in the preamble. When you have a whole series of bills one of whose main objects is the promotion of employment you surely do not have to spell out that phrase in every bill. That is what the measures are all about. They are designed to bolster our economy. That is what they are intended to do. They are intended to promote employment, all of them. To stick that phrase into every bill like a raisin in a fruit cake will not in any way alter or improve the effectiveness of these measures.
We submit that these measures will be effective and that in the main they will have an immediate effect. Certainly they will have a continuity of effectiveness in the years to come. These are co-ordinating measures. They are partnership measures with the provinces, the municipalities and other interested bodies in this country.
All of these measures are a part of the program and each one, I submit, is designed to deal with a specific problem in our

Productivity Council
economy. Unemployment is an economic problem, there is no question about it. It must be cured by economic measures. That is the only way it will be cured. I submit it is not a problem which can be cured by the insertion of pious phrases in our bills. We have tried to avoid pious phrases.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: This whole bill has no content at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
We have brought forward
measures which will put into action the immense economic forces in this country.
In answer to what has been said now, I say there is nothing easier than being destructive. It is easy to get up and say in tones of righteous wrath that this is no good and that is no good. We saw an exhibition of that this afternoon. I think all hon. members recognized the righteous wrath that is usually displayed by the hon. member for Essex East. The hon. member denounced this as no good and that as no good but there was not an indication from him as to what is good. The only suggestion we ever get concerns the setting up of 20 or 22 various committees across the country.
I believe it requires a degree of constructive responsibility to analyse and appraise these measures on their merits and to judge them by their results. As I pointed out earlier, results are already quite evident. I submit there is a favourable response across Canada to all these measures and immediate action is being brought about. I invite hon. members to consider that public confidence is being maintained despite all the words, actions and hopes of hon. members opposite to the contrary.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: The minister is certainly wearing rose-coloured glasses.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. member suggests that I am wearing rose-coloured glasses but at least we on this side of the house can see through them and we are taking measures to rectify whatever we see that is wrong.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: How can a blind man see?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I submit that the productivity council will be useful. I have every faith that it will be a useful council and I have no doubt of the usefulness of such a body in our economy. Certainly, by itself-and I have pointed this out-it will not solve the problem, but we have a number of these measures and when they are put together we have every hope that they will have the desired effect upon our economy. I am sure that they will be beneficial and useful to the people of this country.

Let us examine the position of the hon. member for Essex East. He says the bill is no good; it will have no effect, but he will vote for it.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: For the reasons given.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
He says there are all kinds of things wrong with this bill, but all of the weaknesses will vanish automatically when we put into the bill the phrase that he suggests, "promotion of employment". If we only include those words, all the weaknesses will vanish. All we have to do is to put in these three words and the bill will be perfect because he has submitted the amendment. In other words, what I think the hon. member for Essex East is trying to do is to climb aboard, and he is using this method to do it.
What will this bill do, Mr. Speaker? It will set up a council; that is, a body on which will be represented some of the leading people in our country. It will have on it representatives of all segments of our economic activity. I wish to say that the effort and the aim of this government is to mobilize the economy against insecurity. We are mobilizing the economy on all levels, federal, provincial, municipal, business, industry, agriculture, labour; nobody is left out and nothing is being left out. To do this, in order to bring about this mobilization, we are bringing in measures in the field of housing, construction, municipal aid, the economy, small business, exports, the training of workers, and so on.
I think the hon. member for Essex East will agree that in the main they are all good things. He has some doubts, and possibly hopes that they will not be as effective as we think they will be, and as we hope they will be. Of course, that is something that he has to decide in his own conscience.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: On a point of order, I do not mind what the hon. gentleman says about my arguments but under our rules he has no right to suggest that I have acted in anything but good faith and in accordance with my conscience.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: That is the trouble.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: It is a well established principle of debate that hon. members must assume that their fellow members, like themselves, are acting in good faith and from proper motives.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
That is right; I left it up to the hon. member to decide according to his own conscience. I did not accuse him, or say anything different.

These programs that we have brought forward, calling for the construction of new homes with low down payments, have never been experienced before in this country; programs call for the construction of new training schools; the clearing away of slum areas in our great cities, improvement in the standard of residences and home improvements for our Canadian people; for aid to universities and municipalities and aid to young people, aid for students who wish to advance themselves in the industrial life; the construction of sewage disposal plants across Canada for the preservation of our water resources.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Is this something that the minister is reading from a prepared text?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: The programs call for an opportunity for Canadian businessmen to expand; they call for an opportunity for Canadian businessmen to go into the export markets around the world and to compete there on equal terms through the provision of adequate credit. I submit, Mr. Speaker, this is no "pie in the sky" approach; this is a straightforward, down to earth approach to deal with the problem.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Pious talk.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: It is also a common-sense approach which will bolster up our economy where it is lagging. It will give opportunity to our young people who have not had a chance to acquire a formal education, and it will help business, labour and industry.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the peroration of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) sounded very much like a second edition of the vision and suggests to me once again that instead of having a program of substance the government has given the greatest amount of attention to window dressing and to the package in which its program is being wrapped.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: You should know all about window dressing.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I think the amendment before the house is a straightforward one; it merely calls on the house to express the opinion that in the legislation to set up the productivity council the objective of the work of the productivity council should be the promotion of employment. If we take that as an objective, together with the suggestion that we in this party have made that the productivity council should have the right to make recommendations to the government, we might then be on the way to establishing a body that could take a very active part in assuring full employment and full production.
Productivity Council
I think the Minister of Labour would be much more helpful to the government if he spent less time in demolishing the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and more time in presenting to the house and the country the facts with regard to the government's own program. I suggest the time has come when the Minister of Labour should tell parliament and the country exactly what the government expects will be the result by way of additional employment that flows from all of the projects and all of the legislation that have been presented to parliament at the present time.
We are in a very serious situation in Canada. The government can talk in glib and glowing terms of its action; the fact remains that each passing day that this government has occupied the treasury benches, now for a period of three years, the unemployment situation has become worse. The situation now, according to the latest information, is so bad that we have a higher rate of unemployment than we had in any time during the last 15 years.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: I wonder whether the hon. member would permit a question. I think he is under a misapprehension when he says the last 15 years because surely he is not suggesting it was worse in 1944. It is just for 15 years that we have had these figures.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate will know that at that time demobilization was taking place and there were other reasons why people were looking for work.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: The other reason was the Liberal party.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
We do not want to go too far
back for the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate because his party occupied the treasury benches during a very difficult period of time when they were just as unsuccessful in meeting employment requirements as the present government has been in recent years.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Wait till Tommy Douglas gets in ahead of you.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: The unemployment figure demonstrates not only the number of people who are unemployed in Canada but is an indication of the tremendous loss in production that has taken place as the result of the widespread unemployment. The fact of the matter is that in the last year we have lost by way of production between $1.5 billion and $2 billion of wealth, and so there is a great challenge to the government-

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Can you prove that?

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
-to produce a program that will, in the words of the Minister of Labour,

Productivity Council mobilize the economy against insecurity. The Minister of Labour will not justify his program or his lack of a program by talking about the large numbers of persons now employed. It is not much comfort to the hundreds of thousands who are unemployed to know that there are more employed persons now than there have been in the past. The government's program will be justified when the unemployed have an opportunity to work.
The minister and the government have talked about an over-all program. I want to say that we have been pleased to support this bits and pieces program, this inadequate program, this beginning of a program to meet the present difficulty. There are many other things that I suggest should be done. I think the government should now accept a principle that was enunciated during the war and was accepted by the nation as a whole, namely that anything physically possible would be made financially possible. I think it is physically possible to put Canadians to work and the government should be undertaking those steps that would make this financially possible.
I suggest that there should be established in our country at this time a great capital development fund in the hands of and controlled and operated by the federal government to be used for investment in Canadian industry, to be used for investment in depressed areas and to be used to stimulate our economy, to prime the pump with the objective of bringing about full employment. I suggest also that the government, in co-operation with the provinces, should be prepared at this time to assist in a massive public works program. The federal government has taken certain action in this session to stimulate public works. The fact is that many provincial governments are faced with such budgetary difficulties that they may be compelled to cut back provincial expenditures and thus the provincial governments through no fault of their own will undo much of the valuable work that is being done by the federal government.
The minister talked about the over-all program that the government had presented. He went over the various things that had been done. I suggest that in addition to this program the government should bring into operation once again the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act which was placed on the statute books in 1938 and under which at that time federal money for public works was provided to municipalities at a rate of 2 per cent. This is the kind of far-reaching program for the development of municipal projects that should be brought about at this time, and it should be the purpose and the duty of the productivity council to inquire


into the situation and to make recommendations resulting in the promotion of employment as set forth in the legislation before the house.
The minister talks about his program. I am now trying to suggest to him things that should be added to his program. I suggest that now is the time for the federal government to co-operate with the provinces in a national highway program. Now is the time for the government to cease being content with a contribution to a very limited trans-Canada highway program. The minister has asked for suggestions. He has asked for comments. I suggest that now is the time for the government to undertake measures to bolster farm income which would result in a greater demand for the products of our factories. Now is the time for the government to proceed with its well known commitment to provide for Canada an old age security system which would allow persons to retire on an adequate income.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Order. The hon. member is following in a debate which has been fairly wide but surely there are some limits to what may be discussed on an amendment which only seeks to refer the bill back to the committee to add a clause to section 10 to include in the council's powers the promotion of employment. While I have not objected to the hon. member speaking about employment and unemployment, when he gets into farm income, the trans-Canada highway and other matters it seems to me that a line has to be drawn.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would suggest with great deference that the house listened to the Minister of Labour outline the government's broad program without any objection. He talked about such things as the government measure to provide loans for small business. He talked about the housing program, which is not contained in this legislation. He talked about other measures that the government has brought forward and he challenged the opposition to put forward suggestions. I suggest with great deference that if it is in order for the Minister of Labour to go far beyond the scope of the bill and far beyond the scope of the amendment then, no objection having been raised, the same kind of latitude should be extended to other members in replying to his statement, particularly in view of the fact that he issued a challenge to opposition members to put forward alternative suggestions.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not think I could accept what the hon. member says in total. I have no objection to the hon. member dealing with the matters raised by the hon. member for Essex East and the Minister of Labour

in this debate, that is, the program that the government has brought before the house. Even though that is out of order in this debate it has been discussed, but I do think that a line should be drawn short of the fields to which the hon. member referred.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: I wonder whether I could speak to the point of order and try to assist my hon. friend who is in obvious difficulty. On the government's own figures there has been a considerable drop in agricultural employment over a period amounting to some 300,000. Over the last decade the figure is some 25 per cent less in spite of an increase in production. It would seem to me that because of that circumstance it is not proper for us under our procedures to differentiate between employment in one sector of the Canadian economy as opposed to another. While the hon. gentleman who is speaking is not always in order, I think this is one of the rare occasions when he is.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend from Essex East for his very great assistance. While it was said I am rarely in order I think my batting average is better than that of the hon. member for Essex East. None the less I accept his offer of assistance in the spirit in which it has been given, particularly in view of the fact we must acknowledge his authority in the field of agriculture, soybeans and other related matters.
Now, Mr. Speaker, your ruling was a very interesting one, namely that it is all right to be out of order in fields governed by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) but one must not get out of order in fields outside of those which are of concern to the Minister of Labour.

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman accept a question at this point?

subtopic: PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Fine.

The Minister of Labour referred to the government's housing program, and took great credit for the results he said would flow from that program. I would suggest that the government's housing program has been inadequate and that in the areas of low rental housing, in the provision of housing for senior citizens, it has been very inadequate indeed.
The measure before us would ask the council to inquire inito the development of improved production and distribution methods. We endeavoured, when the house was in committee of the whole, to introduce an amendment which would have widened the scope of the bill and provided for an inquiry into methods to increase markets. I think that is something that this council should consider also. It is not just a question of increasing productivity to bring about full employment, it is a question of developing the markets that are necessary for the products of our industry.
If I may say so at this time, I want to express support for those steps that have been taken by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees).

I was saying I support the measures that have been taken by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the calling of the trade commissioners together to assist in the development of markets for Canadian products. While I expect to have more to say on this particular point at a later time, I feel that the development of markets is essential and that the provision of 20,000 baby chicks for Cuba, reference to which I have seen, is not that kind of expansion of our export trade to Cuba that would require any criticism or opposition from the Liberal party.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that in any inquiry into improved production and distribution methods this council will be forced to look

Productivity Council
at the costs taring our industry today. I think there is nothing that is causing more difficulty, causing higher production costs for the basic industries of our nation at this time than the high interest policy that is being followed by the government. The high interest rates that are prevalent in our country today are making it difficult for our industries to reach their maximum efficiency. The high interest rate coupled with the premium on the Canadian dollar is causing monetary and exchange difficulties that create a great burden for Canadian industry. This is the kind of overhaul of Canadian monetary policy that will be necessary if industries in our country are to reach their most efficient productivity.
What the government has done, Mr. Speaker, has been, useful. What the government has done is no substitute for implementing its promises to the Canadian people to provide job opportunities for all of those who are unemployed.

Have hon. members noticed the delightful argument taking place here today between the leftists under the skin, the brothers under the skin, and this solicitous attitude as if only the leftists are concerned with human beings, in dilating upon the sweet paternity of the state, a socialist heresy which was hatched under the murky atmosphere of the British museum?
The difficulty with regard to discussing employment and unemployment is this. We talk about cold comfort for the unemployed. I cannot imagine any colder comfort than the speeches-if they get around to reading them -of the hon. member for Essex East and the hon. member for Assiniboia. There was an attempt at a last minute amendment which was immediately discarded by its own sponsor who said that notwithstanding the fact that the bill is not a good bill, it was a good bill. The difficulty is that there is so little reasonableness in what we say. We all preach our own little doctrine. When we speak about employment being higher than it was previously, hon. gentlemen on the other side of the house rise in their places and say that this is a weak argument. The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets), who I notice is still in his seat, said this is a weak argument. The hon. member for Assiniboia said this is a weak argument. However, it is part of the economic complex of employment. Those hon. members who want to talk about unemployment talk about unemployment. of representative views who could bring their best information and their best judgment to bear upon the problems of productivity in relation to increased employment and trade.
The other evening we heard a very fine speech from the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh) and this was followed by a guided missive from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). On rereading their speeches I find in them a lingering, archaic economic belief-I do not wish to do the hon. lady any disservice and, if I should do so, I will immediately correct it-
