I can only say to the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) that if it does as well by me in the future as it has in the past I shall be quite satisfied. The theory implicit in this argument put up by the hon. lady and by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is that an increase in productivity at this time will reduce employment. The hon. lady nods her head in agreement, and I am glad that I did her no disservice. But, surely, the result of improving our productivity is to put ourselves in a position where the product of Canadian industry is saleable in world markets, and thereby to increase employment. How else is it to be done? You must improve productivity first of all.
What has the government said? It has said: we shall bring together broadly representative members of industry and commerce, organized labour, agriculture and members of the general public to give the body a leavening of broad interest. We want to bring about a condition in which productivity is improved in order to add to employment in Canada. In this respect it is in line with other measures which have been brought before us during the present session. Consider the National Housing Act. The hon. member for Assiniboia says it is not sufficient. That act has provided a great deal of employment in Canada through a mixture of public and private action by a government which is not fearful of entering into new fields, but will not go down the path of socialist embrace in which all freedom is destroyed.
I see the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) nod his head. I had some things to say about his philosophy during the last session. He nods his head. I was not at Calgary last week, so I do not know where he stood last week, but, surely, we have seen some amazing gyrations in which the far left is suddenly trying to embrace private enterprise. The hon. member for Assiniboia was talking about chickens going to Cuba, and

interest rates, a sort of socialist funny money proposition, but he did not say a word about loans to small business. Wait till some people hear about that, because for the last long while he has been trying to repair that oversight. This arrangement for loans to be made to small business is something for which the small business community in Canada has been asking for a long period of years. The hon. member for Essex East probably thinks that at least the intention of that particular legislation was good. It would, probably, indeed certainly, produce new and vital employment. Then we had a bill-

Well, we have brought into the employment picture a bill providing for the setting up of vocational and technical training institutes. One might ask: what is this going to do for employment? In my city of Halifax we desperately need more vocational training facilities. No less than 77 per cent of the unplaced applicants for employment in Halifax have received education only up to grade eight or less. We desperately need these facilities, and as a member representing that constituency I am grateful to this government for doing something to provide them in order to overcome this serious problem. The distinguished premier of my province was in this city yesterday and announced that a $1,500,000 vocational and technical training institute is to be set up. This will meet a really important need because it will be the means of meeting the challenge of the decade ahead. The situation today is almost ironic, almost an economic contradiction-we have a growing labour force, and more people at work at the same time as we have a growing number of those temporarily disemployed. That is the area which
Productivity Council
this bill seeks to challenge by bringing together the best opinions in the nation under a productivity council to deal with the problem of unemployment.
I believe I have spoken at much less length than hon. gentlemen who preceded me. Mr. Speaker, I just heard an hon. member say: "So as to delay it". May I tell him, through you, Mr. Speaker, that, if the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) knew how to keep silent more often, he might less frequently suffer embarrassment.
On several occasions during the discussion the bill now before us was said not to deal with the unemployed. On the other hand, we were told that the house would be called upon to discuss four measures, of which three have been already passed. This one is therefore the fourth.
A few moments ago, the minister gave us a list of those measures. He told us that those four measures would increase employment in Canada, and thus decrease the number of the jobless. I must say that it is most confusing to listen to the speeches of hon. members on the government benches. They are indeed so confused in their explanations with regard to legislation introduced in this house, that the average man is unable to perceive what they are driving at.
However, the minister has said that these four bills were the basis for the settlement of the present economic problem. Well, Mr. Speaker, I must say that the unemployed cannot eat statistics. They also cannot pay

Productivity Council
their rent with statistics, nor dress their children for school, nor, when they are ill, be treated by means of mere statistics.
Mr. Speaker, it is high time that the government take action, not by merely introducing legislation which will serve as a basis for the settlement of the economic problem, but rather by taking the necessary steps to settle that problem once and for all.
We convened last fall to enact a program which according to the Prime Minister himself, has been ready since September 21. Well, let him submit it to this parliament right now. We have been here since November 17, and all we have seen of this program are the four bills introduced so far as a basis for the solution of the problem which is our concern. That is all. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) and other ministers, and even certain hon. members have said to us: "And you will support the bill".
Well, my reply is quite simple. Mr. Speaker, I was elected to the legislature in 1934, in the darkest days of the depression, when the Conservative government was in power in Ottawa, from 1930 to 1935. I have seen what unemployment means. I perfectly remember the time when people, in groups of 25 to 50, would gather on my verandah in the morning waiting to ask their member for help to buy food, or to be given blankets for their children. I distinctly remember those days and I also know that no Canadian would

want to go through them again. However, I fear that unless the government reaches an early decision on means of correcting the present situation, we will soon be faced with a situation similar to the thirties.
Some will ask why we will support the bill if we think it does not include the provisions needed to settle the problem. To those people I say this: when a jobless man has nothing to eat and is offered hardtack instead of bread, he will take the hardtack. If he is offered treacle instead of maple syrup, he will [DOT]accept the treacle.
Mr. Speaker, let it be understood that if we support these measures, it is because we want to help the government find an answer to the problem. We want to let the government lay the foundation of its program, because that is what the government calls it, a foundation. However, we want more action.

One thing that puzzled me, Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Morris) spoke of Mr. Khrushchev's visit to London is that he forgot to mention that Mr. Khrushchev said if he lived in England he would vote Tory rather than Labour.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it may be trite to say that I am rather unhappy with this bill. I

must go further and say that the situation has not improved as the debate on the bill has progressed. We have seen complete contradictions by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees), the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) even contradicted himself. We have seen vigorous resistance by the government to every attempt to improve this bill. In fact I might say that if the government of the day would attack the problems of the day with the same vigour with which they resist any improvements in their legislation, then we might not be faced with the problems we have today.
We have been told that if we fail to find anything in the bill all we have to do is look in the preamble and we will find it there. As we know, the preamble to any bill is a sort of catchall. In fact, it reminds me very much of some words written by Mr. Wilson MacDonald, when he made reference to the speaker at a service club meeting and went on in these words:
And if the interest seemed to lag He praised the clergy and the flag,
He lauded surgeons and their knives,
He blessed all mothers and all wives.
His talk was like a soothing drug That made men want to kiss and hug;
Or give one hundred thousand bucks To under-privileged woodchucks,
Who got this way, now here's the rub, Because the motto of this club Was ever this-the thought quite missed 'em- That no one must destroy the System.
We have also seen introduced in this bill a brand new principle about which I am certainly not very happy. Under quite close interrogation the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) finally admitted that it is a brand new principle and that it was the first time it had ever been tried in this country. I refer to the system of double taxation on the general taxpayers. That is certainly a novel system of taxation and I do not think it is a good one.
As has been mentioned by innumerable members on the government side, there are in this bill some good measures-I will make that admission-and over a long period of time some good may come out of this bill that is before us today. However, we cannot escape the facts. One of the facts that we cannot get around is that in the United States and Canada at the present time we have the highest productivity of any place in the world; but at the same time that we have the highest productivity we are the only two countries in the western world with an unemployment problem. The reason that we have this problem in these two countries of highest productivity is that we have not given any consideration to the problems that arise through having the highest productivity.

I do not see in this bill anything that is going to change this situation in the future. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, while there may be some good in the long term view I am afraid that as the system is practised in this country the short term harm is going to far outweigh the long term good.

Notwithstanding our disappointment at the refusal of the government to accept either the amendment I moved in committee or the amendment that my friend the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) moved to go back to committee to accomplish the same purpose I had sought to accomplish earlier I want to put on record quite clearly why it is our intention to vote for this measure. I am not going to complicate what I have to say now by going back over any of the other arguments that have been made about the pros and cons of the bill any more than is absolutely necessary, in my opinion, to make this position clear.
In the first place I want to say this. I am unlike the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin), whose views in this matter I respect but do not share. No one in this party has at any time said there was anything positively harmful about this bill. That is a point that I should like to make absolutely clear.
